hints: First ask: can the new shape even hold the numbers? Compare rows·cols with newRows·newCols. If they match, the order of numbers when you read row by row never changes.
Number the cells 0, 1, 2, … in reading order. Cell k sits at (k / cols, k % cols) in grid and must go to (k / newCols, k % newCols) in the new grid — plain index arithmetic, no extra structure.

1. Let rows = grid.length, cols = grid[0].length.
  2. If rows·cols != newRows·newCols, return grid unchanged.
  3. Otherwise create a newRows × newCols grid.
  4. For k from 0 to rows·cols−1, copy grid[k / cols][k % cols] into result[k / newCols][k % newCols].
  5. Return the new grid.

approaches.name: Flatten then refill
approaches.idea: Copy all cells into a 1D list in reading order, then cut that list into rows of length newCols.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: Map each reading-order index k straight from old coordinates to new coordinates with division and remainder.

explain: In the first sample the 2 × 2 grid has 4 cells and 1 × 4 also has 4, so the refold is allowed: k = 0..3 reads 1, 2, 3, 4 and all land in row 0, giving [[1, 2, 3, 4]]. In the second sample 3 × 1 holds only 3 cells, which differs from 4, so grid is returned unchanged. The invariant is that reading order is preserved, which is exactly what the k / width, k % width mapping guarantees.
recognize: "Refill in the same row-by-row order with a new shape" → treat the grid as a flat array and convert indices with / and %.
